content: Thanks for the shout out! We must overhaul Richmond's outdated, exclusive zoning code — and we have a once-in-a-generation opportunity NOW. But only if we speak up! #writetoCityCouncil

I’m for keeping single family zoning. I agree there is a problem, but I don’t think eliminating single family zoning is the solution. Targeted, not blanket rezoning and a focus on derelict homes and structures. Developers won’t build the homes we need, they’ll build to make money and often that means cheaply made but larger sqf homes jammed into small lots.

@arielclark exactly. I think there is also a downward spiral effect. Affordable housing can be addressed by making cheaper housing AND by attracting higher-paying employers. What do higher-paying employers want? Single family neighborhoods that haven’t been retrofitted to accommodate twice the strain on infrastructure. We’re training the public to settle for less instead of demanding more. Beautiful NW neighborhoods are full of vacants. Focus on maximizing our existing housing stock and you’ll attract employers that raise the average pay in the City.

content: @reedinthewind Thanks for the engagement! Actually I agree significantly - targeted zoning, i.e., targeting the city (rather than aiming for the county) allows cities to be more dense and walkable. What single-family zoning means is not just restriction on builders, but on property owners who cannot rent their ADUs or divide their home into a duplex. With single-family-only, the current incentive for builders to only build at the extremes - the McMansions or the big apartment buildings. This zoning reform allows the missing middle housing options to exist in the city.

content:
@arielclark Certainly agree that none of the solutions we're advocating for rely on the ethical bearings of developers. The StrongTowns approach is aimed at incremental, bottom-up solutions made possible by giving greater freedom to residents. That freedom does not extend to controlling their neighbors, but allows them live in arrangements other than single-family.
And I do agree, I love our neighborhoods! Demand is definitely one way to frame it - supply of missing middle options is a big piece of it, too - https://www.strongtowns.org/journal/2026-2-26-three-ways-of-understanding-the-housing-crisis

content: @reedinthewind Re: infrastructure, certainly a valid concern. The main challenge with infrastructure, however, is not the strain of high-density development, but rather the long-term financial insolvency caused by low-density, sprawling development patterns. Utilizing and maintaining existing infrastructure is a more cost-effective model than the suburban sprawl model. Again, the point of zoning reform is to allow the city to be the city; the suburbs can keep doing their single-family only, spread-out, car-centered thing

content: @walkableroanoke yea, I think you need a tighter strategic focus than city/county. More streets in my neighborhood could be rezoned for the missing middle, but others will not work. Also the whole argument: “young people want to buy single family homes but can’t afford them so let’s just eliminate all single family homes” doesn’t seem right. Rezone about 60%? Sure, but have a plan. Restore downtown buildings to build housing, develop vacant land, and see if we still have a problem. Until then, leave the housing stock that people clearly want alone.

content: I’m amazed that amid all the city sponsored events around bike month that city council members who supposedly support sustainability and environmental protections are actually considering these amendments that would require homeowners to add nonpermeable surfaces like driveways to their lots—- there’s no vision for a less car-centric future, no concern for the added flood risks or heat islands, just a plan to appease the wealthy boomers.

@lbcanary there's a sign at the bottom of the ramp off 581 at the downtown exit saying "this is a bicycle friendly city" without a bike lane or crosswalk in sight at one of the worst intersections in the city. I think that about sums up what they think "friendly" means.

content:
We appreciate the shares and signups!
In fairness, I suspect most people who want single-family-zoning-only are worried not about walkability, but rather they are worried about rapid densification (all-the-sudden high rise apts). These reforms actually help us AVOID rapid densification, because it allows for incremental development that increases with demand.
In fairness also in the opposite direction, one of the main backers of the lawsuit against the city (to fight for exclusionary zoning) has publicly criticized those wanting zoning reform by saying derogatory comments about us acting like Roanoke was supposed to be a place like Chicago “where you walk around.” So… those most in the know on all sides I believe understand that walkability requires density, which requires getting rid of restrictive zoning codes that ban all housing except single-family-lots.
The fear is the loss of investment, home values, and neighborhood change. The ironic piece is that walkable, human-scale density (villages, not Manhattans), is so desirable that those places make the land grow in value a ton.

@walkableroanoke just a note. I am against this blanket approach to rezoning and for a walkable/bike-able Roanoke. My main concern is that this strategy relies on developers to build what we want rather than what will make them the most money. I’ve also seen this type of retrofit damage bikeability. Build new denser neighborhoods where we can start from the ground up (Evans spring), take a measured and strategic approach to rezoning based on clear criteria and develop incentives for derelict housing improvement (which is a money making investment). Respectfully.
